```python
def count_rotation(arr):
    # The rotation count is the index of the smallest element. In a rotated
    # ascending array, that element sits right after the first descent.
    for i in range(len(arr) - 1):
        if arr[i] > arr[i + 1]:
            return i + 1
    return 0


assert count_rotation([3, 2, 1]) == 1
assert count_rotation([1, 2, 3]) == 0
assert count_rotation([3, 1, 2]) == 1
assert count_rotation([2, 3, 1]) == 2
assert count_rotation([4, 5, 1, 2, 3]) == 2
assert count_rotation([]) == 0
```

This is the same code as before. It assumes distinct elements, which is the GfG setup. It runs in O(n) time with O(1) extra memory.

I did not follow the team note saying the answer is "the number of elements after the minimum." For `[3,2,1]` the minimum is at index 2 with nothing after it, so that rule returns 0 and fails your first assert. A binary search for the minimum index also returns 2 there, so it would fail too. The first-descent rule is the one that matches all your asserts.
